abstract: Mäkelä and Stephany examine whether AI acts as a substitute or complement to human labor by analyzing 12 million online job vacancies from the United States spanning 2018-2023. The study takes a dual approach, examining both internal effects (within AI-focused roles) and external effects (across industries and occupations exposed to AI adoption). The findings strongly favor complementarity: AI-focused positions are nearly twice as likely to require resilience, agility, or analytical thinking compared to non-AI roles. Data scientists with resilience or ethics capabilities receive 5-10% higher salary offers. A doubling of AI-specific demand correlates with a 5% increase in demand for complementary human skills even outside AI-related roles. Overall, complementary effects are up to 1.7 times larger than substitution effects. Results are consistent across the United States, United Kingdom, and Australia.
keyFindings: AI-focused positions are nearly twice as likely to require resilience, agility, or analytical thinking compared to non-AI roles, indicating AI adoption drives demand for distinctly human capabilities.
Data scientists with resilience or ethics capabilities receive 5-10% higher salary offers, demonstrating a measurable wage premium for complementary human skills in AI-adjacent roles.
A doubling of AI-specific demand correlates with a 5% increase in demand for complementary skills even outside AI-related roles, showing spillover effects across the broader labor market.
Complementary effects of AI on human skill demand are up to 1.7 times larger than substitution effects, suggesting net positive impact on demand for human capabilities.
Results are consistent across the United States, United Kingdom, and Australia, providing cross-national validation of the complementarity finding.
methodology: Empirical analysis of 12 million online job vacancies from the United States (2018-2023), with cross-national validation using UK and Australian job posting data. The study measures both internal effects (skill demands within AI-focused roles) and external effects (how AI adoption in industries affects demand for complementary skills in non-AI roles). Regression analysis links AI exposure measures to changes in skill requirements and wage offers.
qualifiers: arXiv preprint, not yet peer-reviewed. Job postings capture employer demand signals but not actual hiring outcomes or worker experiences. The 2018-2023 period captures early AI adoption and may not reflect longer-term equilibrium effects. Online job vacancy data may underrepresent certain sectors or occupation types. The complementarity finding at the skill-demand level does not preclude net employment losses at the occupation level if some roles are entirely automated.
